summary: Defines the WebDAV Access Control Protocol, new methods, headers, properties and reports that let a client read and change access control lists on web resources. These say which principals may do which operations. Principals are represented as web resources, and searches help find them.

eli5.summary: On a shared online folder, someone decides who can look at or change each file. This adds the web commands for setting those permissions.

questions: how to set permissions with webdav
how does the webdav acl method work
subtitle: How a WebDAV server says who may read, write or change the permissions of each web resource.

tldr.problem: WebDAV let clients author content on web servers, but there was no interoperable way to read or change who is allowed to do what with each resource.
tldr.mechanism: Each resource gets an access control list (ACL) of entries that grant or deny privileges to principals, which are themselves web resources. A new ACL method sets the list, properties read it, and four reports help find principals.
tldr.outcome: Clients can show and edit permissions on any compliant server. The RFC leaves out roles, per-property access control, ACL initialization and global ACLs.

today: RFC 3744 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
The goal of the WebDAV access control extensions is an interoperable way to handle discretionary access control for content and metadata managed by WebDAV servers. The principle is that who you are determines what you may do to a resource. A principal says who you are, and a single access control list (ACL) on each resource says what you may do.

An ACL holds access control entries (ACEs). Each ACE names a principal and a set of privileges that are either granted or denied. When a request arrives, the server walks the ACEs to decide whether the principal may perform that HTTP or WebDAV method.

Authentication is intentionally left to HTTP, but some mechanism must be available. HTTP Digest Authentication is the one that all WebDAV compliant implementations are required to support. Out of scope are access control for a single property, role-based security, how an ACL is initialized, an ACL that applies globally, and creating or maintaining principals and groups.
sections.eli5: Every file has a guest list. The list names people and says what each may do. The server checks the list every time someone asks to do something.

sections.title: Principals and Groups
sections.content:
A principal is a network resource that represents a distinct human or computational actor that initiates access to network resources. Users and groups are the usual examples. A URI of any scheme MAY identify a principal, but servers MUST expose each principal at an http or https URL, which has the extra properties the RFC defines.

A group is a principal that represents a set of other principals. Membership is recursive: if a principal is in group GRPA and GRPA is in GRPB, the principal is also in GRPB.

A principal can have several URLs, and a client cannot tell that two URLs name the same one. The RFC therefore requires clients to use the single URL in the DAV:principal-URL property when writing ACEs. Every principal must also have a non-empty DAV:displayname so a person can recognize it. The DAV:group-member-set and DAV:group-membership properties list direct members of a group and the groups a principal belongs to, and DAV:alternate-URI-set can point to more descriptive resources such as an LDAP URL.
sections.eli5: People and teams each get their own web address. A team counts as one name, and its members count as the team too. Everyone must use one official address for each name so nobody gets mixed up.

sections.title: Privileges
sections.content:
The ability to perform a method on a resource MUST be controlled by one or more privileges. The RFC defines well-known ones: DAV:read (GET, PROPFIND and OPTIONS), DAV:write (such as PUT and PROPPATCH), DAV:write-properties, DAV:write-content, DAV:unlock, DAV:read-acl, DAV:read-current-user-privilege-set, DAV:write-acl, DAV:bind, DAV:unbind and DAV:all. Servers MAY add their own, but not in the DAV: namespace.

An aggregate privilege contains other privileges, so granting it grants each one inside it. A privilege may be abstract, which means it cannot be set in an ACE on that resource. A server that cannot separate reading content from reading the ACL can declare both abstract and group them under a non-abstract aggregate. Privilege containment loops are not allowed.

Some containment is forbidden to keep things distinct. For example DAV:read-acl MUST NOT contain DAV:read or DAV:write, and DAV:write MUST contain DAV:bind, DAV:unbind, DAV:write-properties and DAV:write-content. A client denied access gets 403 "Forbidden", except that 404 "Not Found" may be used when the privilege restricts knowing the resource exists.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big key, there are small keys: one to look, one to change, one to delete, one to change the guest list. Some keys come on a ring, so getting the ring gives you all the keys on it.

sections.title: Access Control Properties and ACEs
sections.content:
Access control information is read like any other WebDAV property, with PROPFIND. Because it can be expensive for a server to compute, a PROPFIND allprop request SHOULD NOT return these properties. Resources that support the protocol MUST have them.

  • DAV:owner and DAV:group name a principal as owner or group of the resource.
  • DAV:supported-privilege-set is a protected property listing the privileges defined for the resource as a tree, with descriptions tagged by xml:lang.
  • DAV:current-user-privilege-set lists what the current user has been granted, so a client can gray out actions the user cannot perform.
  • DAV:acl is the list of ACEs itself.
  • DAV:acl-restrictions tells clients what the server will refuse, for example grant-only (no deny ACEs), no-invert and deny-before-grant.
  • DAV:inherited-acl-set names other resources whose ACLs must also grant a privilege; the privileges are ANDed.
  • DAV:principal-collection-set points to the root collections of principals.

An ACE names its principal as an href, or as DAV:all, DAV:authenticated, DAV:unauthenticated, DAV:self or a DAV:property such as DAV:owner. It may wrap the principal in DAV:invert, then contains DAV:grant or DAV:deny, and may carry DAV:protected (cannot be removed) or DAV:inherited (comes from another resource and is changed there).
sections.eli5: The guest list is stored as a note on the file. Each line says a name, and either yes or no, and for which keys. Some lines are locked in place or copied from the folder above.

sections.title: How an ACL Is Evaluated
sections.content:
ACLs are evaluated in a similar manner to ACLs on Windows NT and in NFSv4. ACEs are kept in order and checked until every permission the request needs has been granted, and then access is granted. If a deny ACE that matches the current user covers a privilege not yet granted, evaluation stops and access is denied. Failing to have all required privileges means denial.

Mixing grant and deny ACEs lets the model express other systems. The RFC shows the UNIX r--rw-r-- scheme as an ACL: the owner gets read and then everything else is denied to the owner, the group gets read and write and then everything else is denied to the group, and all principals get read.

The RFC also changes existing methods. Every HTTP method gains a DAV:need-privileges precondition, so a 403 response body can say which resource lacked which privilege. A server MUST return access-control in the DAV header of an OPTIONS response. A MOVE must not modify the non-inherited, non-protected ACEs, a COPY gives the destination the ACL a new resource would get, and a LOCK protects only the ACEs a client can modify.
sections.eli5: The server reads the list from top to bottom. If it finds a yes for everything you asked, you are in. If it finds a no first, you are out.

sections.title: The ACL Method and Principal Reports
sections.content:
The new ACL method replaces all non-inherited and non-protected ACEs on a resource with exactly the ACEs in the request body, which MUST contain one DAV:acl element. If the new list cannot be applied exactly, the request MUST fail. A client SHOULD lock the resource before reading the ACL it plans to update, to avoid overwriting another client's change. To add or remove one ACE, a client reads the ACL with PROPFIND, drops inherited and protected ACEs, edits the rest and sends it back.

A failed request returns 403 or 409 with a named precondition inside DAV:error. Examples include DAV:no-protected-ace-conflict, DAV:no-inherited-ace-conflict, DAV:deny-before-grant, DAV:no-abstract, DAV:recognized-principal and DAV:missing-required-principal. A compliant server MUST support at least one ACE for a single principal and one for a group.

Four reports use the REPORT method from RFC 3253, which all compliant servers must support through DAV:expand-property. DAV:acl-principal-prop-set returns chosen properties, such as display names, for the principals in an ACL. DAV:principal-match finds resources whose principal matches the current user, for example everything the user owns. DAV:principal-property-search finds principals by searching properties such as DAV:displayname; the preferred default is a caseless substring match. DAV:principal-search-property-set says which properties can be searched.
sections.eli5: One command rewrites the guest list. Other commands help you look up people by name, so you can find the right name to put on the list.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC names three risks. First, a single compromised user who can change ACLs across many resources can alter far more than before, so write-acl privileges across broad ranges should go to few people.

Second, readable ACLs help attackers. If all resources have world-readable ACLs, a PROPFIND with Depth infinity can efficiently find resources left world-writable, which could then be overwritten repeatedly. The RFC advises not to grant read-acl to unauthenticated principals, and notes that exposing DAV:current-user-privilege-set trades usability against security.

Third, the protocol deliberately does not say how an initial ACL is set, so a creator may find undesirable privileges, and for a short time the resource exists with that initial ACL. On authentication, the Basic and Digest mechanisms of RFC 2617 apply, and Basic, if used, MUST only be supported over secure transport such as TLS.
sections.eli5: If a thief gets the key to the list, they can change who gets in. Anyone who can read the lists can also spot unlocked doors. So share the power to change lists with very few people.
